title: Singleness: A Bible Study for the Unmarried
subtitle: A five-session study on singleness, calling, and belonging.
summary:
This study is for single people, for the widowed and the divorced, for the ones who chose singleness and the ones who did not, and for the small groups and churches that have too often left them standing in the lobby. It walks slowly through five sessions on singleness as a calling and not a deficiency, on desire and loneliness and the honest ache that no one should be shamed for feeling, on chastity as a way of honoring a body that is good and not dirty, on the family that is wider than the nuclear one because the church is a household before it is a collection of couples, and on the contentment and the real fruitfulness of a life that never stops being able to bear fruit. It is built so a busy leader or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the ache the single person carried into the room already.

This study is written by a married man, and that is exactly the problem it means to confront first. Bell is a pastor with a wife and five sons, and he writes from inside the honest admission that men like him have built the church for men like him. He has planned the sermon series around marriage and the potluck around families and the small group around couples, and he has left the single people in his church to feel like the meeting had not started yet, like they were waiting for their real life to begin. He does not point at that failure from a safe distance. He is the one who committed it. So he writes not as an authority on a life he has not lived but as a brother repenting of a blindness he did live, and he lets the single voices in Scripture, Paul and Jesus and the prophet Jeremiah, carry the weight he cannot. The one thing this study will not do is treat singleness as a lesser Christianity or a holding pattern for the not-yet-married. It will honor the person content in it and it will sit honestly beside the person aching in it, and it will never, on any page, tell either one that they are half of something waiting to be completed. They are whole. The gospel says so, and the church has to learn to say it too.
audience: Single adults, the widowed and divorced, and the churches and groups that carry them

sessions.title: A Calling, Not a Deficiency
sessions.aim: To name singleness as a genuine calling honored by Scripture and lived by Jesus himself, not a deficiency to be cured by marriage or a waiting room where real life is on hold, and to refuse both the church's quiet assumption that everyone is meant to pair off and the cynicism that treats the single life as a failure to launch.
sessions.summary: A woman in her late thirties told Bell, after another wedding where she had been seated at the table in the back with the other unmarried guests, that she had begun to feel like a problem the church did not know how to solve. She was not bitter. She was describing a message she had received a hundred small ways, that the single life is a phase you pass through on the way to the real thing, and that until you arrive you are somehow unfinished. The real question is not whether it is hard to be single in a church built for couples, but what singleness actually is, because a deficiency you try to cure and a calling you try to steward are two entirely different lives. Scripture does not treat singleness as a deficiency. Paul calls it a gift, plainly, and wishes more people could receive it. And the single person Scripture holds up above all others is Jesus, who was unmarried, and whom no one would dare call incomplete. Bell takes the strong case for the other view, that God said it is not good for the man to be alone, that marriage is the creation norm and singleness the exception, that pushing singleness as equally good ignores a real design. There is truth in it that he will not dodge. But the creation word about aloneness was never a word about marriage as the only cure, and the New Testament opens a calling the Old Covenant could barely imagine, a life freed for the kingdom in a way marriage is not. The single life is not the waiting room. For some it is the whole house, built on purpose, and God is the one who drew the plans.

keyScripture.why: I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another. Paul names both marriage and singleness as gifts from God, refusing to rank the single life beneath the married one and calling his own unmarried state a gift he wishes more could receive.

discussion.q: Bell says the church quietly teaches that the single life is a phase you pass through on the way to the real thing. Where have you received that message, and what did it do to how you saw your own life?
discussion.behind: Open on the felt experience before any theology. Single people have absorbed this in a hundred small ways, the seating at weddings, the sermon illustrations that assume a spouse, the questions about when they will settle down. Name the message honestly first, and let the married people in the room hear how loudly the church has said a thing it never meant to say out loud. Land it on honesty, not on defending the church.

discussion.q: Paul calls singleness a gift from God, and the single person Scripture holds highest is Jesus himself. What changes when you hear that the most complete human life ever lived was an unmarried one?
discussion.behind: Move to the theological center. Most people have never let it register that Jesus, the fullest human being who ever lived, was single, and that no one would call his life unfinished or half. Help the room feel that if singleness were a deficiency, the incarnation is inexplicable. The point is not to win an argument but to let the pressure off, to let the single person hear that their state is not a lack Jesus came to fix but one he shared.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that God said it is not good for the man to be alone, that marriage is the creation design. What is true in that you do not want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness, and protect the aching person too. The creation word is real, and marriage is a genuine good, not a consolation prize, and the study must never sound like it is talking single people out of a real desire. Make sure no one hears the session as a command to be content on demand or as a dismissal of the longing for marriage. Honor the design and the desire before showing what the New Testament adds to both.

discussion.q: If singleness is a calling to be stewarded rather than a deficiency to be cured, what would it look like to actually build a life on it instead of waiting for a life to begin?
discussion.behind: Push from diagnosis toward imagination. The waiting-room posture keeps the single person from planting anything, buying the house, taking the calling, putting down roots, because it all feels provisional until marriage arrives. Invite the room to picture a single life built on purpose rather than held in reserve. Do not let it become a pep talk. The aim is a real shift from provisional to planted.

discussion.q: Bell confesses that as a married pastor he has built the church around couples and families and left single people feeling like the meeting had not started yet. Where have you, single or married, treated singleness as the lesser state?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and let the leader go first. This includes the single people, who often believe the diminishment about themselves more deeply than anyone imposes it. It includes the married, who assume without malice that their arrangement is the norm everyone is headed toward. Grace means nothing until the assumption is named in the room, gently, including in the leader's own heart.

objections.objection: God himself said it is not good for the man to be alone. Marriage is the creation design and singleness is the exception at best, so calling them equally good just flatters people who have not managed to find a spouse.
objections.response: Sit with the truth in it, because it is real and worth granting fully. Marriage is a genuine creation good, not a consolation prize, and the longing for it is not immaturity but the echo of a real design, and no one should be talked out of that ache or made to feel foolish for it. Grant all of that without hedging. Then notice what the objection assumes and Scripture does not, that marriage is the only cure for the aloneness God named. The word in Genesis is spoken before there is any church, any covenant community, any resurrection, into a world with two people in it, and it is answered in the New Testament in a way that could not be seen from Eden. Jesus, unmarried, was not alone, and Paul, unmarried, calls his state a gift he wishes others shared, a life freed for the kingdom. The creation word is true. It simply was never a decree that marriage is the single person's only escape from being alone, because the deepest belonging was always meant to be found in God and his people, and marriage was always a sign of that, never the source.

objections.objection: This all sounds nice, but the honest truth is that single people in the church are just people who have not found anyone yet. Dressing it up as a holy calling is a way of making a disappointment sound spiritual.
objections.response: Hear the honesty, because it names something the church's cheerful language often papers over, that for many people singleness is not chosen and does carry real disappointment, and pretending otherwise is its own cruelty. Grant that plainly. Then press on the word calling, because a calling is not the same as a preference, and Scripture does not make it one. Paul did not choose his singleness because he failed at dating. He received it as a gift and stewarded it for the kingdom, and the church has always known men and women who did the same, some by circumstance and some by design, whose single lives bore fruit a married life could not have borne. A calling can be one you did not ask for and would not have chosen and still be genuinely from God, the way Jeremiah did not choose his hard word and Paul did not choose his thorn. The disappointment is real. So is the calling. They are not enemies, and naming the second does not deny the first.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the life you have been quietly refusing to start, the thing you have told yourself you will do once you are married, and what would it mean to begin it now as though this life were already your real one?
sessions.practice: This week, name one place you have lived as though your real life were still ahead of you, the roots you would not put down, the calling you would not take, the home you would not make your own, and take one concrete step to plant it now. Buy the thing for the house. Say yes to the work. Do not wait to begin living until a wedding gives you permission. And privately, whether you are single or married, ask God to show you where you have believed singleness is a lesser life, and write down what he brings up.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us for belonging, and in your Son you showed us a single life so full that no one would dare call it incomplete. Forgive us for teaching, in a hundred quiet ways, that the unmarried life is a waiting room and the married life the only real one. Forgive the churches that seated the single ones in the back and called it hospitality. Teach us to receive singleness the way Paul did, as a gift and a calling and not a diagnosis, and teach the married among us to repent of the assumption we never knew we made. Let no one in this room believe they are half of something. In Christ they are whole, and their life has already begun. Amen.
reflection: Where have I believed, or made others believe, that the single life is a phase to pass through rather than a life to live?
If Jesus lived the fullest human life ever lived and never married, what does that say about the completeness I thought marriage would give me?
What have I refused to plant, build, or begin because I was waiting for a marriage that would make my life feel like it had finally started?
sessions.teaching: A woman in her late thirties told Bell, after another wedding where she had again been seated at the table in the back with the other unmarried guests, that she had begun to feel like a problem the church did not know how to solve. She was not bitter, and she was not exaggerating. She was reporting, accurately, a message she had received in a hundred small and unintended ways, that the single life is a phase you pass through on the road to the real thing, and that until you reach it you are somehow unfinished, a sentence with no period, a house with the framing up and no one living in it. We begin there, because before we ask whether singleness is hard, which everyone knows it is, we have to ask what it actually is, and the answer decides everything about how a person lives it. A deficiency is something you try to cure. A calling is something you try to steward. Those are not two moods about the same life. They are two entirely different lives. And here is the plain fact the church keeps managing not to notice. Scripture does not treat singleness as a deficiency. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, calls it a gift from God, using the same word he uses for the gifts of the Spirit, and then says the startling thing, I wish that all were as I myself am, that he wishes more people could receive the very state the modern church treats as a waiting room. And then there is the fact that should have settled this two thousand years ago and somehow never did. The single person Scripture holds highest, the fullest and most complete human being who ever drew breath, was unmarried. Jesus of Nazareth never married, and no one, in two millennia, has dared to call his life incomplete or half or provisional. If singleness were a deficiency, the incarnation is unintelligible, because God, given a whole human life to live and every option in it, chose to live it single. Take the strong case for the other view, because thoughtful people make it and it is anchored in the text. God himself said, in the second chapter of Genesis, that it is not good for the man to be alone. Marriage is written into creation, blessed at the start, called very good, and there is a real design here that a glib egalitarian shrug about singleness can dishonor. Grant it fully. Marriage is not a consolation prize and the ache for it is not immaturity, it is the echo of something true, and I will not have this study talk anyone out of a longing God himself planted. But watch what the objection quietly assumes that Scripture never says. It assumes marriage is the only cure for the aloneness God named. Read the word again. It is spoken before there is a church, before there is a covenant people, before there is a resurrection, into a world containing exactly two human beings, and it is answered across the whole of the New Testament in a way that could not possibly have been seen from Eden. Jesus, unmarried, was not alone. Paul, unmarried, was not incomplete. The deepest belonging a human being can know was always meant to be found in God and in his people, and marriage, good as it is, was always a sign pointing to that belonging, never the source of it. Here is where I have to stand inside the failure, because the writer is inside this indictment before the reader is. I am a married pastor with a wife and five sons, and men like me built the church for men like me. I planned the sermon series on marriage and the seminar on parenting and the small group around couples, and I seated the single people, without ever deciding to, in the back of my own imagination. I made the potluck a family event and the retreat a couples getaway and then wondered why the unmarried members drifted. I treated their singleness, without a word, as the thing we were all quietly hoping God would fix for them. I repent of that here, in print, because I cannot teach this honestly from above it. The single life is not the antechamber to the Christian life. For Paul it was the Christian life, lived at full stretch, freed for the kingdom in a way he says marriage is not. For some in this room it is not a phase and not a delay and not a problem to be solved. It is the whole house, built on purpose, and the God who drew the plans for it is the same God who called his own Son to live it. That is not a life waiting to begin. That is a life already underway, and the only thing waiting is the church, waiting to finally honor it.

scriptureStudy.note: It is not good that the man should be alone. The word names a real human need for belonging, but it is spoken before church, covenant, or resurrection, and the New Testament will answer the aloneness with more than marriage, with God and a people.

I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God. Paul calls both singleness and marriage gifts, using the language of grace, and refuses to rank one beneath the other. Singleness is not a lack of the gift of marriage but a gift of its own.

To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single as I am. Paul says plainly it is good to remain single, not tolerable, not second-best, good, and he includes the widowed, those whose singleness came by loss.

There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Jesus names a deliberate, honored singleness undertaken for the kingdom, a life given up for a reason, and says let the one who is able to receive this receive it.

To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, I will give in my house a monument and a name better than sons and daughters. God promises the childless and unmarried a name in his house greater than descendants, overturning the old assumption that offspring were the measure of a life.

The word of the Lord came to me: You shall not take a wife. God called the prophet Jeremiah to a singleness he did not choose, as a sign to the people, proof that a called singleness can be hard, unchosen, and still unmistakably from God.

There is no one who has left house or wife or brothers for the sake of the kingdom who will not receive many times more. Jesus promises that what is surrendered for the kingdom, including the married life, is repaid many times over, now and forever.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session only gestures at, because the church did not always treat singleness the way much of the modern American church now does. For most of Christian history the single life was held in unusual honor, sometimes to a fault. The early and medieval church so exalted celibacy that it risked demeaning marriage, and a group should grant that the overcorrection was real, that treating the single life as spiritually superior did its own harm. But notice what the Protestant recovery of marriage, right and needed as it was, quietly cost. In lifting marriage back to its proper dignity, much of the Protestant world swung so far that it left singleness with almost no positive vision at all, until the unmarried Christian became a person merely waiting, and the church that once revered its celibates could barely imagine why anyone would choose that life. Set this against the plain fact that the two figures at the center of the New Testament, Jesus and Paul, were both single, and that the movement they founded spread in no small part through the freedom of unmarried men and women to go where a family could not follow. A group can weigh this carefully against the genuine good the Reformation recovered, holding both truths, that marriage is honorable and that the church lost something when it forgot how to honor the single. Then take the harder turn. The modern West has made romantic partnership the assumed center of a meaningful life, so that a person without it is read, by the wider culture and too often by the church, as lonely or unfulfilled by definition. This is not a Christian idea. It is a cultural one, and the church absorbed it without noticing. The aim is not to despise marriage, which is good, but to see how a whole civilization came to treat coupledom as the one door to a full life, and to ask where that assumption got into the church's bloodstream without permission, and whom it has quietly wounded.
sessions.caseStudy: A single man in his forties in your group is settled, faithful, and useful in the church, and when the session turns to singleness as a calling he stiffens, not out of pain but out of principle. He says he does not want to hear his singleness called a gift, that it feels like a spiritual spin put on a disappointment, that he has prayed for marriage for twenty years and calling it a calling feels like being told to be grateful for the thing he grieves. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it presses him. He is not wrong that the church often uses the word calling to shut down a real grief, and you should say so plainly and mean it. The longing he carries is not a lack of faith, and no one should hand him a slogan for it. But notice what he has assumed, that a calling is only a calling if you chose it, when Scripture is full of callings no one asked for, Jeremiah's singleness among them. Help him see that naming his life a calling does not deny his grief, it dignifies it, because a gift you did not choose and would not have chosen can still be genuinely from the hand of God and genuinely fruitful. Do not let him collapse the whole matter into whether he is happy about it. Honor the grief fully, and still ask him, gently, whether the years he has called wasted might be the very years God has been working through.

sessions.title: Desire, Loneliness, and the Honest Ache
sessions.aim: To make room for the genuine ache of singleness, the desire for a spouse and the loneliness of a life without one, without shaming the person who feels it and without pretending faith makes it disappear, and to refuse both the false cheer that denies the pain and the despair that lets the pain have the last word.
sessions.summary: Bell says the cruelest thing the church does to single people is not the seating chart, it is the pressure to pretend the ache is not there. A young man who admitted he was lonely was told he just needed to be content in Christ, as though the loneliness were a sin to repent of rather than a wound to be met. The real question is what to do with the desire and the ache that will not go quiet, because two lies compete for the single heart, and both are cruel. The first says the ache is a lack of faith, that a truly surrendered believer would feel no longing. The second says the ache is the truth about your life, that you are alone and always will be, and it lets the loneliness write the verdict. Bell takes the strong case for the first, that Scripture does command contentment, that Paul learned to be content in any circumstance, that endless indulgence of longing can become its own kind of bondage. There is real wisdom in it. But contentment is not the absence of ache, and the Bible never pretends it is. The Psalms are full of holy people telling God exactly how much it hurts, and Jesus himself, in the garden, did not deny his anguish, he named it. Then the reversal. The ache is not the enemy of faith. Very often it is the form faith takes in a longing heart, the desire aimed, finally, at the God who is the only one who can hold it. You do not have to choose between the false cheer and the despair. There is a third thing, older than both, the lament that tells the truth about the pain and still reaches for God with it.

keyScripture.why: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. The verse names the third way between denial and despair, the pouring out of the honest heart, ache and all, before a God who is a refuge and not a judge of the pain.

discussion.q: Bell says the cruelest thing the church does is pressure single people to pretend the ache is not there. Have you felt that pressure, and what happened to the ache when you had to hide it?
discussion.behind: Open on the felt reality, gently, because this is tender ground and some in the room have never been allowed to say it out loud. The pressure to perform contentment does not remove the loneliness, it drives it underground where it festers. Make the room safe for honesty first. Let people name the ache without anyone rushing to fix it, and go first if the silence is heavy.

discussion.q: Two lies compete for the single heart, that the ache means you lack faith, and that the ache is the final truth about your life. Which of the two has had more power over you, and how do you hear it talking?
discussion.behind: Help the room name its particular lie. Some are crushed by the guilt of feeling lonely at all, believing a real Christian would not. Others have surrendered to the loneliness as a verdict, that no one will ever come, that they are fundamentally alone. Naming which lie has the loudest voice is the first step to answering it, and most people, pressed, will recognize one more than the other.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that Scripture commands contentment and that Paul learned to be content in any circumstance. What is true in that, and where does the call to contentment get twisted into a command to feel no pain?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The command to contentment is real, and endless wallowing in longing can become a bondage of its own, and the study must not license self-pity. But contentment is not the absence of ache, and turning it into that is exactly the cruelty of the first lie. Help the room hold the genuine call to contentment together with the genuine permission to hurt, because Scripture holds both without strain.

discussion.q: The Psalms are full of holy people telling God exactly how much it hurts, and Jesus in the garden named his anguish rather than denying it. What would it change to bring your loneliness to God as lament instead of hiding it as sin?
discussion.behind: Move toward the recovery of lament, which most modern Christians have lost. The Psalms model a prayer that tells God the unvarnished truth about the pain and still addresses him, which is neither denial nor despair. Help the room see that the honest complaint is not a failure of faith but a form of it, and that God is not fragile before their ache. Invite them to imagine praying the loneliness rather than burying it.

discussion.q: Bell says the ache is very often the form faith takes in a longing heart, the desire finally aimed at the God who alone can hold it. Where might your deepest longing be pointing you past the thing you want toward the God you actually need?
discussion.behind: Close on the reversal and the gospel. This is not a trick to make the desire for marriage disappear by relabeling it. It is the older truth that every earthly longing is finally a longing for God, that the ache for a spouse is real and also points past itself to a belonging only God completes. Let the room feel the desire honored and redirected at once, and end in weight, not in a neat resolution.

objections.objection: If I am supposed to be content in Christ, then the fact that I am still lonely and still want to be married must mean my faith is weak. A stronger Christian would not feel this ache at all.
objections.response: Take the fear seriously, because it is doing real damage, and then dismantle it, because it is not from God. Nowhere does Scripture teach that faith removes desire or that a holy person feels no ache. The Psalmists were men and women after God's own heart, and they told him, at length, exactly how much their lives hurt. Jesus, the only person who ever had perfect faith, sweat and pleaded in the garden and did not pretend his anguish away. If perfect faith did not erase the ache in him, imperfect faith was never going to erase it in you, and expecting it to is not humility, it is a burden Scripture never laid on anyone. Contentment, the thing Paul actually learned, is not the absence of longing. It is the presence of God inside the longing, the settled trust that holds even while the desire aches. You are not failing because you still want what God made you to want. You would be lying if you said you did not. Bring the ache to him honestly. That is not weak faith. It is where faith actually lives.

objections.objection: Telling me my loneliness points me to God is just a way of spiritualizing away a real problem. I do not want a theological lesson. I want another human being who does not leave, and pretending God fills that need feels like a dodge.
objections.response: Grant what is honest and even right in this, because it is closer to the truth than the false cheer that provoked it. The desire for another human being who does not leave is good, and God-given, and this study will not pretend that a private devotional life is a full substitute for a body in the next room and a hand to hold. That longing is real and it deserves to be taken seriously, not lectured away. Where the objection needs a gentle push is in the false choice it assumes, that it is either God or a person, spiritual comfort or real presence. Scripture does not answer the loneliness of the single with God alone in a private room. It answers it with God and a people, a family wider than the nuclear one, a household of brothers and sisters meant to be a real and embodied belonging, which the next sessions will press hard. The dodge is not the claim that God meets you. The dodge is a church that says God will meet your loneliness and then fails to be the family through which he meets it. The problem is real. So is the answer, if the church will be it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the ache you have been hiding, even from God, because you were afraid that feeling it at all meant your faith had failed, and what would it be like to finally say it out loud to him?
sessions.practice: This week, do the thing you have been told not to do. Take the loneliness and the longing directly to God, out loud or on paper, and tell him the unvarnished truth about how much it hurts, the way the Psalmists did, without editing it into something more spiritual first. Do not resolve it. Just bring it. And if you have been carrying the ache alone, tell one trusted person, not to be fixed but to be known, and write down what shifts in you when the ache is finally spoken instead of buried.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us to long, and then you told us we could bring the longing to you without shame. Forgive the church for teaching single people to hide the ache and call the hiding faith. Forgive us for treating loneliness as a sin to repent of instead of a wound to be met. Teach us the lost prayer of lament, to tell you the truth about how much it hurts and to keep reaching for you inside the hurt, the way the Psalmists did and your own Son did in the garden. Meet the lonely ones in this room, not with a lecture but with your presence and with a people who will be your hands. And take our deepest longing and aim it, finally, home to you. Amen.
reflection: Which lie has had the louder voice in me, that the ache means my faith has failed, or that the ache is the final truth about my life?
Have I ever brought my loneliness to God as honest lament, or only tried to hide it from him and pretend it was already resolved?
If every earthly longing finally points past itself to God, what might my desire for marriage be trying to tell me about the belonging I most need?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the cruelest thing the church does to its single people is not the seating chart at the wedding or the family-only language in the bulletin, painful as those are. It is the quiet, relentless pressure to pretend the ache is not there. A young man in his church once admitted, with real courage, that he was lonely, that the empty apartment at the end of the day pressed on him, and he was told, kindly and disastrously, that he just needed to learn to be content in Christ, as though the loneliness were a sin to be confessed rather than a wound to be met. So we have to begin with the ache itself and ask what a single person is supposed to do with a desire and a loneliness that will not go quiet no matter how much they pray, because two lies compete for the single heart, and both of them are cruel, and most people are being crushed by one or the other. The first lie says the ache is a failure of faith, that a truly surrendered believer would feel no longing, that if you still want to be married and still feel the loneliness at night, your walk with God must be shallow. This lie produces guilt on top of grief, a person hurting and then ashamed of hurting. The second lie is the opposite and just as cruel. It says the ache is the whole truth about your life, that you are alone and always will be, that the loneliness is not a feeling but a verdict, and it invites the single person to sink into it and let it write the story. Take the strong case for the first lie, because there is a real and biblical truth it has distorted. Scripture does command contentment. Paul says he learned, in whatever situation, to be content, that he knew how to be brought low and how to abound. Endless indulgence of a longing, turning the desire over and over until it becomes the center of the whole self, really can become a kind of bondage, and the study will not pretend that wallowing is the same as honesty. Grant all of that. But here is what the first lie cannot survive. Contentment, in the Bible, is never once described as the absence of ache. The same Scripture that commands contentment gives us a hundred and fifty Psalms, and a great many of them are the prayers of holy men and women telling God, at length and without editing, exactly how much their lives hurt. How long, O Lord. My tears have been my food day and night. These are not the prayers of weak faith. They are the prayers the Holy Spirit inspired and preserved as the model for how God's people talk to him about pain. And then there is the garden. Jesus, the only human being who ever had perfect faith, knelt in Gethsemane and did not deny his anguish or spiritualize it away. He named it. My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. If perfect faith did not erase the ache in the sinless Son of God, then the expectation that your imperfect faith will erase it in you was never humility. It was a burden no one in Scripture was ever asked to carry. Now the reversal, and it is the whole point. The ache is not the enemy of faith. Very often the ache is the form faith takes in a longing heart. Because every earthly desire, if you follow it far enough, turns out to be pointing past itself. The hunger for a spouse who will not leave is real, and good, and God-given, and it is also, underneath, the hunger of a creature for the only One who finally never leaves, the belonging that marriage was always a sign of and never the source. So you do not have to choose between the false cheer that denies the pain and the despair that surrenders to it. There is a third thing, older than both of them, and the church has nearly forgotten it. It is called lament. It tells God the whole truth about the ache and keeps reaching for him with it, refusing both the lie that says do not feel this and the lie that says nothing but this is true. I have to say plainly that as a married man I have been part of the machinery of the first lie. I have offered a lonely person a verse and a smile when what they needed was for me to sit in the silence with them and let the ache be real in the room. It is easier to fix a feeling than to feel it alongside someone. The gospel does not fix the ache by making it disappear. It meets the ache with a God who took on a human heart and let it break, and who says to every longing, hidden or spoken, pour it out before me, I am a refuge and not a judge of your pain.

scriptureStudy.note: Pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. The verse gives permission most Christians never claim, to bring the unedited heart to God, and calls him a refuge for the one who does, not a judge of the pain poured out.

My tears have been my food day and night. The Psalmist grieves openly, thirsting for God, and the honesty is not rebuked but recorded as inspired prayer, proof that lament is a form of faith and not a lapse from it.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Jesus, with perfect faith, names his anguish in the garden rather than denying it, which settles forever the lie that a strong enough faith would feel no ache.

I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. Paul's contentment is learned, not automatic, and it is the presence of God inside the circumstance, not the absence of any hard feeling about it.

Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. The Psalmist's desire, honestly wrestled through, lands finally on God himself as the portion no loss can take, the longing arriving home.

God settles the solitary in a home. God takes personal responsibility for the loneliness of the solitary, promising to set them in a home, which in the New Covenant becomes the household of his people.

My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Paul's unremoved thorn teaches that God often meets an ache not by taking it away but by meeting the person inside it with sufficient grace.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the recovery of lament, because the modern church, and the American church especially, has largely lost a language its own Scriptures are saturated with. Roughly a third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint and grief addressed directly to God, and yet they are nearly absent from contemporary worship, which prefers the triumphant and the upbeat. A group should weigh what this loss has cost, because a church with no room for honest grief will always tell its hurting members, single or otherwise, to paper over the pain, and the single person carrying an unmet longing is among the first casualties of a faith that has forgotten how to say how long, O Lord. Set this against the biblical pattern, in which lament is never the opposite of faith but one of its truest expressions, the refusal either to deny the pain or to abandon God because of it. Then bring in the wider cultural diagnosis, tested against Scripture. The modern West is, by many honest secular accounts, experiencing an epidemic of loneliness, and the researchers who name it are describing something real, the fraying of the bonds of family, neighborhood, and church that once held people. The secular account gets the symptom right, the ache of isolation is genuine and widespread, and it gets the anthropology only half right, because it treats the loneliness as a problem to be solved by better networking rather than as the deep signal of a creature made for a belonging no network provides. A group should hold both, letting the research name the scale of the wound and letting Scripture name its depth, which is that the human heart is restless until it rests in God and in the people he gives. The aim is to recover a faith honest enough to grieve and hopeful enough to keep grieving toward God, and to refuse the false comfort that would rush a lonely person past a pain the Bible itself would sit down inside.
sessions.caseStudy: A single woman in your group has quietly stopped coming to the parts of the ache that hurt most, and when the session turns to loneliness she says, a little too quickly, that she is fine, that she gave all of this to God years ago and does not struggle with it anymore. The room can feel that the door has just been closed. Here is the work for the leader, and it requires gentleness above everything, and no prying. She may genuinely be at peace, and you must not insist on a wound she is not carrying, because assuming every single person is secretly devastated is its own condescension. But the quickness of the fine, the practiced surrender that shuts the conversation rather than opening it, is worth a gentle notice, because the pressure to perform contentment often sounds exactly like this. Do not challenge her in front of the group. Honor what she said and let it stand publicly. But make a private moment available, and if she takes it, do not offer a verse, offer your presence, and let her know that the ache, if it is there, is not a failure and does not need to be hidden from you or from God. The aim is not to manufacture a grief she does not feel. It is to make sure that if the grief is there, she knows there is finally a room, and a God, that can hold it.

memoryVerse.text: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us.

sessions.title: Chastity and the Body Without Shame
sessions.aim: To recover chastity as the honoring of a body that is good, not the denial of a body that is dirty, to take sexual faithfulness in singleness as a positive discipline of the whole self rather than a list of prohibitions, and to refuse both the culture's lie that the body is only appetite and the church's old lie that the body is only danger.
sessions.summary: Bell says the church handed single people the hardest possible teaching in the worst possible way, telling them to keep their bodies pure while making them feel that their bodies were the problem. The result is a generation that heard do not and never heard why, that connected chastity with shame instead of with honor. The real question is what the body is for, because the culture says it is an appetite to be satisfied and the old church said it was a danger to be suppressed, and Scripture says something both of them miss, that the body is good, made by God, bought at a price, and a temple of his Spirit. Chastity, then, is not the hatred of the body. It is the honoring of it, the refusal to let a good thing be spent as though it were nothing. Bell takes the strong case for the modern view, that sexual expression is a natural part of being human, that lifelong celibacy for the involuntarily single is a heavy and even cruel demand, that the church has caused real damage with its shame and its silence. He grants every bit of the damage. But the modern cure, treating sex as an appetite like hunger, does not honor the body, it cheapens it, because the body was never only an appetite, it was always a place where the whole self is present. Then the reversal and the self-implication. The problem was never that the church asked too much of single bodies. It is that the church asked it with contempt instead of honor, and offered no vision of a chaste life that is anything but deprivation. Chastity is not less than the culture's freedom. It is the harder and higher freedom of a body kept whole for the sake of a love it is still learning to trust.

keyScripture.why: Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. Paul grounds chastity not in the body's shame but in its astonishing worth, a temple, purchased, indwelt, to be honored and not spent as though it were nothing.

discussion.q: Bell says the church taught single people to keep their bodies pure while making them feel their bodies were the problem. Where did you learn to connect chastity with shame instead of honor, and what did that do to you?
discussion.behind: Open on the tender history, carefully, because this is the most vulnerable session and some carry real wounds here. Many heard only the prohibition and absorbed a shame about the body itself. Make the room safe and unembarrassed, keep it from becoming crude or clinical, and let people name the shame they were handed before the session offers the honor Scripture actually teaches. Do not rush past the wound.

discussion.q: The culture says the body is an appetite to satisfy and the old church said it was a danger to suppress. What does it change to hear Scripture call your body good, bought at a price, and a temple of the Spirit?
discussion.behind: Move to the theological center, which is the reframe the whole session turns on. Both the culture and the shaming church made the body a lesser thing, one to use and one to fear. Scripture makes it a temple. Help the room feel the weight of that word, that chastity guards something precious rather than restraining something dirty. The aim is relief and dignity, not a higher bar of prohibition.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that lifelong celibacy for the involuntarily single is a heavy and even cruel demand and that the church has done real damage with its shame. What is true in that you want to honor?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves with real care, and protect the people carrying the heaviest version of this. The demand is genuinely heavy, especially for those who did not choose singleness, and the church's shame did real harm, and none of that should be minimized. Make sure no one hears the session as a glib insistence that chastity is easy. Honor the weight and the wound fully before showing what makes the discipline bearable and even good.

discussion.q: If chastity is honoring a good body rather than denying a dirty one, how does that change the way you would actually live it, day to day, rather than just white-knuckling a list of prohibitions?
discussion.behind: Push from theology toward lived practice. A chastity built only on do-not is exhausting and shame-soaked and usually fails. A chastity built on honoring something precious is a positive discipline of the whole self, of attention and habit and community, not just of the body in a moment. Help the room imagine the difference between suppressing an appetite and stewarding a temple, and what that looks like on an ordinary lonely Tuesday.

discussion.q: Bell says the church asked much of single bodies but asked it with contempt instead of honor. Where have you, in yourself or toward others, treated the single body as a problem rather than a temple, and what would honor look like instead?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and let the leader go first. This includes the married, who often pity or quietly judge the celibate single, and the single, who may have absorbed contempt for their own bodies. The gospel meets us not with contempt but with the staggering worth of a body bought at a price. Name the contempt honestly, in the room and in the leader's own heart, before offering the honor.

objections.objection: Sexual expression is a natural, healthy part of being human, and telling involuntarily single people they must be celibate for life, maybe forever, is not holiness. It is a cruel and unrealistic demand that produces only shame and repression.
objections.response: Grant the weight of it first, because the demand really is heavy and the church has often made it heavier by adding shame to difficulty. Lifelong celibacy that no one chose is a hard road, and pretending it is easy, or that a truly holy person feels no cost, is its own cruelty, and the church owes repentance for the shame and silence it has piled on top of the difficulty. Grant all of it. Where the objection goes wrong is in the word natural, and what it assumes follows from it. Many desires are natural and are still not meant to be acted on wherever they arise, and the fact that a longing is real and God-given does not mean its satisfaction is owed. Chastity does not deny that the desire is natural. It says the body in which the desire lives is worth more than the culture's account of it, a temple and not an appliance, and that keeping it whole is not repression but honor. The demand is heavy. The church should carry it alongside the single, not lay it on them and walk away. But heavy is not the same as cruel, and the alternative on offer, a body spent as though it were nothing, honors the person less, not more.

objections.objection: The church's whole obsession with virginity and purity has done enormous psychological damage, teaching people, especially women, that their worth is their sexual status. Why should I trust anything the church says about my body?
objections.response: Do not defend the damage for a second, and say so first, because the damage is real and largely the church's own doing. The purity teaching that tied a person's worth, and a woman's worth above all, to her sexual status was a distortion and a wound, and it made the body a source of shame rather than a gift, and the anger at that is not sin, it is closer to justice. Grant it fully. Then notice that the cure for a lie about the body is the truth about the body, not the abandonment of the subject to the culture, which has its own lie ready. Scripture never grounds your worth in your sexual status. It grounds your worth in being made by God, bought at the price of the cross, and indwelt by his Spirit, which is true of the virgin and the non-virgin, the faithful and the fallen, exactly alike. Chastity in that frame is not a scorecard of purity that determines your value. It is the free honoring of a body whose value was already settled, unconditionally, at the cross. The church owes an apology for the lie. It also owes you the truth it buried underneath it, that your body was always worth more than either the shamers or the culture ever told you.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What did you learn to believe about your own body, and is it the culture's lie that it is only an appetite, the old church's lie that it is a danger, or the truth that it is a temple bought at a price and worth honoring?
sessions.practice: This week, examine the story you have been telling yourself about your body, and test it against the one Scripture tells, that it is good, made by God, bought at a price, a temple of his Spirit. Where you find shame, bring it to God and ask him to replace it with honor. And practically, look honestly at the habits and inputs that make chastity harder, the screen, the scroll, the isolation, and change one of them this week, not to earn purity but to guard something precious. Write down what changes in you when you treat your body as a temple rather than a problem.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made our bodies and you called them good, and then you did the astonishing thing, you bought them at the price of your Son and made them temples of your Spirit. Forgive the church for teaching single people to guard a thing while despising it, for handing them prohibition without honor and shame without truth. Heal the wounds that teaching left. Teach us that chastity is not the hatred of the body but the honoring of it, not repression but reverence for something you paid for. Give the single ones in this room the harder and higher freedom of a life kept whole, and give them a church that carries the weight alongside them instead of laying it on them and walking away. Glorify yourself in our bodies, which are yours. Amen.
reflection: What story did I absorb about my body, and does it match the story Scripture tells, that it is good, bought at a price, and a temple of the Spirit?
Have I lived chastity as the shamed suppression of a dirty thing, or as the glad honoring of a precious one, and what would change if it were the second?
Where have I let contempt, my own or the church's, fall on the single body, mine or someone else's, that God calls worth the price of the cross?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the church handed single people the single hardest teaching it has, and it handed it to them in the worst possible way. It told them to keep their bodies pure, and at the same time, in a thousand tones and glances and badly aimed sermons, it made them feel that their bodies were the problem, that desire itself was shameful, that the flesh was a dirty thing to be beaten into submission. The result is a generation of believers who heard the word do not and never once heard the word why, who came to associate chastity not with honor but with shame, and who, when the prohibition finally cracked, felt not only that they had broken a rule but that they had confirmed a suspicion about themselves the church had planted years before. So we cannot start with the rule. We have to start further back, with the question the rule never bothered to answer, which is what the body is actually for. The culture has a confident answer. The body is an appetite, and appetites exist to be satisfied, and a satisfied appetite is health and a denied one is repression. The old shaming church had the opposite answer and it was no better. The body is a danger, a field of temptation, a thing to be suppressed and gotten through until the soul can be free of it. And Scripture, as usual, says a third thing that both of them entirely miss. It says the body is good. God made it and called it good before there was any fall to complicate it. And then it says something that should stop every shaming sermon in its tracks. Your body, Paul tells the Corinthians, is a temple of the Holy Spirit. You are not your own. You were bought with a price. Not a danger to escape. Not an appliance to use. A temple, indwelt by God himself, purchased at the cost of the cross. Once you see that, chastity turns inside out. It is not the hatred of the body. It is the honoring of it. It is the refusal to spend, as though it were nothing, a thing that God valued at the price of his own Son. Take the strong case for the modern view, because it is reacting to a real and grievous failure and it deserves an honest hearing. It says that sexual expression is a natural and healthy part of being human, that to demand lifelong celibacy of a person who never chose singleness, perhaps forever, is a heavy and even cruel thing, and that the church has done enormous damage with its shame and its silence and its obsession with a purity it made into a scorecard. Grant it. Grant all of it. The demand is heavy, heaviest of all for the person who did not choose the single life and did not want it, and I will not stand here as a married man and pretend the cost is small. And the damage the church did is real, especially to women, whose worth it too often tied to their sexual status as though a person were a sealed or broken container. That was a lie and it wounded people and the church owes repentance for it, not a defense. But watch where the modern cure fails, because it fails the body it claims to free. Treating sex as an appetite like hunger does not honor the body. It cheapens it. Hunger is satisfied by any food, and if the body is only an appetite then any partner will do and none of it means anything, and the very thing the culture promised would liberate the body ends by emptying it of significance, until the most intimate act a person can perform says nothing at all. The body was never only an appetite. It was always a place where the whole self is present, which is exactly why what is done with it matters so much. And now I have to stand inside the church's failure, because I am part of the institution that committed it. The problem was never that the church asked too much of single bodies. The demand, rightly framed, is not too much. The problem is that the church asked it with contempt instead of honor. It said keep yourself pure and communicated your body is a danger. It offered the single person a life of prohibition with no positive vision of what a chaste life is for, nothing but a long deprivation to be endured until marriage rescued them from it, which for many would never come. As a married pastor I preached the rule and never once painted the beauty, told single people what to say no to and never showed them the yes underneath it, the whole self kept whole, the body honored as a temple, the love that is worth waiting for even if it never arrives in this life because its truest fulfillment is in the next. So hear the reversal. Chastity is not less than the culture's freedom. It is a harder and a higher freedom, the freedom of a body not spent, kept whole for the sake of a love it is still learning to trust, honored because it was bought at a price. The single Christian keeping chastity is not repressing a dirty thing. They are guarding a temple. And the church that asked it of them owes them, at the very least, the honor of saying so, and the honesty of carrying the weight alongside them instead of setting it on their shoulders and walking away.

scriptureStudy.note: God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. The body is included in the very good of creation, before any fall, which means it is good at the root, not a shameful thing to be escaped or suppressed.

Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Chastity is grounded in the body's worth, not its shame, a temple purchased at the cross and indwelt by God, to be honored rather than spent.

This is the will of God, your sanctification, that each of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor. Paul pairs holiness with honor, framing sexual self-control as the honoring of the body, not the despising of it.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases. Scripture treats desire as good and powerful and worth guarding, not denying its force but honoring its right time, which affirms the body even as it counsels patience.

Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. The body is the very instrument of worship, offered to God whole, which makes chastity an act of worship rather than mere restraint.

But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion. Paul is realistic about the weight of the desire and refuses to shame it, treating the longing as real and marriage as a good and honorable answer to it for those called to it.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Purity in Scripture is finally of the heart and aimed at seeing God, not a scorecard of the body, which frees chastity from the shame of a status and roots it in communion with God.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the theology of the body, because the recovery this session needs is not a stricter rule but a truer account of what a body is. Christianity has always had to fight on two fronts at once, against the ancient error that despised the body as a prison of the soul and against the modern error that reduces the body to a machine for pleasure, and a group should notice that the shaming church and the liberating culture are, underneath, making the same mistake, treating the body as a lesser thing, one to escape and one to use. The Christian claim cuts against both, that the body is good, that the resurrection of the body is central to the faith, that God himself took a body and kept it forever, and that therefore what a person does with the body is neither trivial nor shameful but weighty and honorable. Set this against the ancient heresy the early church fought hardest, the various forms of teaching that the material world and the body were evil or illusory, and notice that a chastity built on that old error was always going to produce shame rather than honor, because it was never fully Christian to begin with. Then bring in the cultural diagnosis, tested against Scripture. The sexual revolution of the twentieth century promised that detaching sex from commitment and consequence would free the body, and by many honest secular accounts the result has not been simple liberation but a rise in loneliness, in the commodifying of persons, and in a widespread sense that intimacy has become both more available and less meaningful. The secular account, at its most honest, is beginning to name a disappointment it did not expect, that a body treated as an appetite turns out to be a body that no longer means anything, and Scripture named that outcome long before, when it said the body is a temple and warned against spending it as though it were not. The aim is to hold both truths, the goodness of the body and the weight of what is done with it, and to recover chastity as reverence for something precious rather than fear of something dirty, so that the single Christian keeping it is not enduring a shame but guarding a temple.
sessions.caseStudy: A single man in your group carries a heavy, quiet shame, and when the session names chastity he grows tense, because he has not kept it, and every mention of purity lands on him as a verdict he has already passed on himself. He does not say much, but you can see the word purity hitting him like an accusation. Here is the work for the leader, and it must lead with the gospel before it says one word about the standard. He needs to hear, first and unmistakably, that his worth was never his sexual record, that it was settled at the cross before he ever succeeded or failed, and that the God who calls his body a temple bought that body at a price that no failure can revoke or reduce. Do not let the session hand him one more scorecard, because the scorecard is the very lie that wounded him. Only after grace has actually landed, after he knows he is not standing in the dock, can the honor of chastity be offered to him again, not as a status he lost but as a life still open to him, because the temple was never destroyed, only forgotten, and the God who owns it is in the business of restoring what was spent. Honor the shame by taking it to the cross, and refuse to let purity be preached to him as anything other than grace.

memoryVerse.text: For you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.

sessions.title: Family Beyond the Nuclear
sessions.aim: To recover the church as a household and a family before it is a collection of couples, to name the single person not as an outsider to family life but as a full member of the deepest family there is, and to refuse both the idolatry of the nuclear family that leaves the single stranded and the isolation that lets the single settle for a Christianity of one.
sessions.summary: Bell says the church made an idol of the nuclear family and then wondered why its single people felt homeless. It built its language and its calendar and its imagination around the household of husband, wife, and children, until the person without one was, by definition, a person without a place. The real question is what family actually is in the New Testament, because the church has assumed the answer is the nuclear household, and Jesus assumed something far larger and stranger. When told his mother and brothers were outside, Jesus looked at the people around him and said, here are my mother and my brothers, whoever does the will of God. He relativized the biological family in favor of a deeper one, the family of faith, and the early church took him at his word, calling each other brother and sister and meaning it. Bell takes the strong case for the family, that the nuclear household is God-ordained and good, that a church which dissolves it into a vague collective loses something precious, that children need a mother and a father. He grants all of it. But honoring the family is not the same as making it the ceiling of belonging, and when the church treats the nuclear household as the highest and only real family, it has quietly demoted the very family Jesus said was deepest. Then the reversal and the self-implication. The single person is not on the outside of family looking in. In the household of God they are a full member of the truest family there is, and the tragedy is not their singleness but a church that forgot how to be the family it was supposed to be. Belonging was never meant to depend on a wedding. It was meant to depend on a baptism.

keyScripture.why: For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother. Jesus names the family of faith as a real and primary family, not a metaphor, making every believer, married or single, a full member of a household deeper than blood, which is the belonging the single person was always meant to have.

discussion.q: Bell says the church made an idol of the nuclear family and then wondered why its single people felt homeless. Where have you seen the church build its life around the household of husband, wife, and children, and what did that do to the ones without one?
discussion.behind: Open on the felt experience. The idolatry is rarely stated, it is in the calendar, the language, the assumptions, the family ministries with no place for the single adult. Let the single people name where they have felt homeless in a church that never meant to exclude them, and let the married hear it. Land it on honesty about a real blindness, not on blame.

discussion.q: When told his family was outside, Jesus pointed to the people around him and called them his mother and brothers. What is your honest reaction to Jesus relativizing his own biological family in favor of the family of faith?
discussion.behind: Move to the theological center, which is startling and often softened. Jesus really did place the family of faith above blood, and modern Christians, who have half-sacralized the nuclear family, often flinch at it. Help the room take the saying at full strength, that the family of faith is not a lesser, metaphorical family but a real and primary one. The point is to expand belonging, not to demean the household.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that the nuclear family is God-ordained and good and that a church which dissolves it loses something precious. What is true in that you want to keep?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The family is a genuine good, children do need mothers and fathers, and a church that vaguely dissolves the household into a collective loses something real. The session must not sound anti-family. Honor the goodness of the nuclear household fully before showing how making it the ceiling of belonging strands the single. Protect the married and the parents in the room from hearing an attack on their calling.

discussion.q: Bell says belonging was never meant to depend on a wedding but on a baptism. If the single person is a full member of the truest family there is, what would a church actually look like that lived as though that were true?
discussion.behind: Push from theology toward imagination and practice. If the church is a real family, then single people are not guests at other people's family life but members of one. Ask the room concretely, what would change in the calendar, the language, the homes, the holidays, if the household of God were treated as a real household. Do not let it stay abstract. Belonging that is real is embodied, in kitchens and at tables.

discussion.q: Bell confesses that as a married pastor he built a church where belonging depended on having a family of your own. Where have you, single or married, treated the nuclear family as the real family and the church as merely an event you attend?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and let the leader go first. The married often retreat into the nuclear household and treat the church as a service they consume. The single sometimes settle for a Christianity of one, isolated, expecting nothing of the family they belong to. Both have shrunk the family of God to something less than Jesus meant. Name it honestly, in the room and in the leader's own household.

objections.objection: The nuclear family is the bedrock of society and it is under enough attack already. The last thing the church should do is relativize it. Children need a mother and a father, and a vague talk of the church family is no substitute for the real thing.
objections.response: Grant the good you are defending, because it is real and worth defending. The nuclear family is a genuine, God-ordained good, children do flourish with a mother and a father, and a church that dissolves the household into a vague and formless collective has lost something precious and owes the family its honor. Grant all of that without hedging. Where the objection slips is in hearing relativize as demote, when Jesus did neither of those things to demean the family. He did it to reveal a family deeper than blood, the household of God, of which the nuclear family is a good and honored part but never the whole. The problem this session names is not too much love for the family. It is an idolatry that made the nuclear household the ceiling of belonging, so that the person without one was left with no family at all, which is a thing Jesus never intended and the early church never allowed, calling one another brother and sister and meaning it enough to share their homes and their tables and their goods. Honoring the family and being a real family to the single are not enemies. The same church is called to both, and a church that does only the first has not honored the family too much. It has understood the family of God too little.

objections.objection: The idea of the church as my family sounds warm but it is not real. When I am sick, or lonely on a holiday, or need someone at two in the morning, the church family is nowhere to be found. My actual family shows up. The church does not.
objections.response: Take this with total seriousness, because it is not cynicism, it is testimony, and it indicts the church far more than it indicts the doctrine. You are right. Too often the church family is a warm phrase and not a real presence, absent exactly when a real family would show up, at the hospital, on the holiday, in the two a.m. crisis. That is a genuine failure, and the honest response is not to defend the church but to repent for it. But notice where the failure actually lies, because it is not in the teaching, it is in the church's disobedience to it. The New Testament does not describe the family of God as a sentiment. It describes it as brothers and sisters who shared their homes, carried each other's burdens, and were commanded to treat the older as parents and the younger as siblings, in the flesh, with keys and casseroles and rides to the hospital. When the church family fails to show up, the problem is not that the doctrine overpromised. It is that the church underdelivered on a promise Christ actually made. The answer to a church that fails to be a family is not to abandon the idea of the family of God. It is to become the thing we have only been saying, and it starts with the person reading this deciding to be family to someone before demanding the church be family to them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who in the family of God are you actually family to, in the embodied ways a real family is present, and if the honest answer is no one, what has kept you at the edge of a household you already belong to?
sessions.practice: This week, act on the truth that the church is a real family and not an event. If you are single, do not wait to be included, move toward the household, invite someone into your home or ask to be in theirs, be a brother or sister to someone in the flesh. If you are married, open your family to a single member of the church, not as a charity but as kin, a standing seat at the table, a place at the holiday. And whoever you are, find one person to whom you will be family this week in an embodied way, and write down what it costs and what it gives.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you are building a household, and you told us plainly that the family gathered around your will is deeper than the family gathered around a bloodline. Forgive the church for making an idol of the nuclear family and leaving your single members homeless in your own house. Forgive us who are married for retreating into our households and treating your church as an event we attend. Teach us to be the family we keep only saying we are, brothers and sisters in the flesh, with tables and keys and casseroles and presence at two in the morning. Let no one in this room belong to you and still feel they belong to no one. Their belonging was never a wedding away. It was settled at their baptism. Make us live as though we believed it. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated the nuclear family as the only real family and the church as merely an event I attend rather than a household I belong to?
Do I take Jesus at his word that the family of faith is a real and primary family, or do I quietly treat it as a lesser, metaphorical one?
To whom am I actually family in the embodied ways a real family is present, and whom have I left at the edge of a household they already belong to?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the church made an idol of the nuclear family, and then it stood there genuinely puzzled about why its single people felt homeless. It never decided to exclude anyone. That is the thing about idolatry, it rarely announces itself. It simply built its language and its calendar and its whole imagination around the household of husband, wife, and children, until the sermon illustration assumed a spouse, the ministry was called family ministry, the retreat was a couples retreat, the small group was full of pairs, and the potluck was a gathering of clans, and the person who arrived without a household of their own discovered, without anyone having to say it, that there was no obvious place for them to stand. So we have to ask the question the church skipped, which is what family actually is in the New Testament, because the church has quietly assumed the answer is the nuclear household, and Jesus, it turns out, assumed something far larger and considerably stranger. There is a scene that ought to unsettle every church that has half-sacralized the nuclear family. Jesus is teaching, and word comes that his mother and his brothers are outside, asking for him. And he does the thing that no defender of family values quite knows what to do with. He looks around at the ordinary people sitting in front of him and he says, here are my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother. He does not despise his biological family. But he plainly relativizes it. He names a family deeper than blood, the family of faith, and he calls it his real mother, his real brothers, and he means it. And the early church took him at his word in a way that should embarrass us. They called each other brother and sister, and it was not a nickname. They shared their homes and their tables and their possessions, they carried one another's burdens, and Paul told Timothy to treat the older men as fathers and the younger as brothers, the older women as mothers and the younger as sisters, which is only a strange instruction if you have forgotten that the church was supposed to be a household with actual kinship in it, and not a weekly event that people with real families attend. Take the strong case for the family, because it is good and it is under real pressure and it deserves a full and honest defense. The nuclear family is God-ordained. Children do need and flourish with a mother and a father. A church that dissolves the household into a vague, formless collective, that treats marriage and parenting as interchangeable or optional or passe, has lost something precious and dishonored a genuine gift of God. Grant every bit of it. This session is not an argument against the family, and any single person tempted to hear it as permission to resent married people and their children should hear that the family is a good thing God made, not a rival to be torn down. But now watch the distinction the objection walks right past, because everything turns on it. Honoring the family is not the same as making it the ceiling of belonging. And that is exactly what much of the church did. It took the nuclear household, which Jesus called a good and honored part of the family of God, and it made it the whole, the highest, the only real family, so that the person without one was left, by the church's own logic, with no family at all. In doing that, the church did something worse than exclude its single members. It quietly demoted the very family that Jesus said was the deepest one there is. It made the family of blood higher than the family of the blood of Christ. Here is where I have to stand inside it, because I built one of those churches. As a married pastor with a wife and five sons, I made a church where belonging, without my ever intending it, depended on having a family of your own. I planned for households and preached to households and left the single members to attend the family I had built for everyone but them. And when they drifted, I told myself they were struggling with contentment, when the truth is they were struggling with homelessness, in a house I had failed to make a home for them. So hear the reversal, and let it land where it should. The single person is not standing on the outside of family, looking in through the window at everyone else's real life. In the household of God they are a full member of the truest family there is, brother and sister to every believer, sons and daughters in a house whose Father does not forget the solitary but settles them in a home. The tragedy of Christian singleness was never the singleness. It was a church that forgot how to be the family it was always supposed to be, and left people who belonged to it feeling as though they belonged to no one. Belonging was never meant to depend on a wedding. It was meant to depend on a baptism. And every single person who has ever felt like a guest in the family of God was told a lie by a church that had forgotten its own doctrine, because they were never a guest. They were always kin.

scriptureStudy.note: Who are my mother and my brothers? Whoever does the will of God. Jesus names the family of faith as a real and primary family, deeper than blood, making every believer a full member of a household that does not depend on marriage or descent.

God settles the solitary in a home. God himself takes responsibility for the belonging of the single and the solitary, promising to place them in a home, which in the New Covenant is the household of his people.

Treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters. Paul commands the church to relate as actual family, with the roles and obligations of kin, which only makes sense if the church is a real household and not an event.

You are no longer strangers and aliens, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God. Belonging in the church is framed as membership in a household, not attendance at a gathering, and it is grounded in Christ, not in one's marital state.

To the eunuchs I will give in my house a name better than sons and daughters. God promises the childless and unmarried a place and a name in his house greater than biological descendants, overturning the assumption that family by blood is the measure of belonging.

They had all things in common, and breaking bread in their homes. The early church lived its kinship in the flesh, sharing homes, tables, and goods, which is the embodied family the New Testament describes and the modern church too often reduces to a sentiment.

Let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith. The church is called the household of faith and given the obligations of a household, to care for its own with the concrete provision a family gives, not the distance of an institution.
